messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 55-year-old fashion designer who came to treatment after years of insisting he had simply become “difficult” with age. He grew up in a house where danger arrived through the person meant to protect him. His caregiver’s physical abuse was unpredictable, often happening in stretches of unnatural quiet that made him listen for footsteps, a shift in breathing, the touch of a hand on his shoulder that could turn, without warning, into violence. What remained with him was not a single clean account but broken sensory fragments and a bodily certainty that silence meant something bad was about to happen. Even now he cannot tell a clear story of what happened from beginning to end. At times he can describe an incident in a flat, detached way, as if he were talking about someone else’s childhood, and then without warning a shard of memory brings a surge of guilt so strong that he feels implicated in his own suffering.

As an adult, David built a life around beauty, control, and presentation. In his studio, where assistants move around him pinning fabric and adjusting garments on models, he has become known for flinching sharply if someone touches him from behind. He covers it with irritability or precision, but inside the reaction feels immediate and absolute. He has come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that something in him was permanently altered by what happened. The fact that he still startles, still scans even his own apartment at night, has convinced him at times that he may be going crazy. Those beliefs do not sit quietly in the background; they shape how he moves through the world, leaving him on guard at home and especially unsettled by silence, which feels less peaceful than ominous, as though it is the moment before something terrible begins again.

The memories and the meaning he makes of them feed each other. Because the abuse comes back in disconnected pieces, David takes the gaps as evidence of damage: if he cannot form a coherent story, he thinks, then his mind must be broken. When he recalls the past in an emotionless, almost foreign way, that numbness frightens him as much as the content itself; it seems to confirm his fear that he has been changed for the worse. And when guilt arrives during recall, he turns it inward and outward at once, dwelling on what he must have done wrong while also circling for hours around what other people did to him and how unprotected he was. The more he remembers in fragments, the more mistrustful and self-condemning he becomes.

Over time David developed rituals to manage this. He avoids times of day and situations that he associates with nightmares, delaying sleep with work, television, or pacing around the apartment rather than lying in the dark when the quiet closes in. He ruminates constantly—sometimes accusing himself, sometimes replaying the injuries done by others—because he feels that if he could only think hard enough, he might finally make sense of it or assign blame correctly. These habits are driven by his beliefs that people are dangerous, that he has been permanently damaged, and that his reactions signal mental collapse. Yet the effect is the opposite of relief. By refusing the times that bring dreams and by spending hours trapped in repetitive blame, he never arrives at a fuller narrative; the memory remains jagged, numb in places and contaminated by guilt in others. Each failed attempt to think his way through it leaves him more convinced that something is fundamentally wrong with him.

His state of alarm also pulls the past closer. On nights when his apartment falls silent, he checks locks, listens for sounds in the hallway, and feels watchful even in bed. After an unexpected touch at work—a seamstress brushing his arm to get his attention, a model stepping too close backstage—he can spend the rest of the day with old fragments pressing in, not as a complete recollection but as bodily knowledge and flashes he cannot organize. That renewed contact with memory deepens his conviction that he is unsafe and unstable. In turn, those convictions heighten his vigilance, making silence more menacing and ordinary contact more startling.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had begun to cost him professionally and personally. Assistants had started avoiding him because his sharp reactions to touch felt hostile, and his adult daughter had told him that being in his apartment was exhausting because he was always listening, always tense. What finally brought him in was a recent night when he sat awake until dawn to avoid dreaming and found himself thinking, with unusual clarity, that he could not keep living as if the danger were still in the room. He is most afraid that the damage is permanent and that his mind is slipping beyond his control, but he is also hoping, cautiously, that if he can understand what happens to him when the silence comes, the past may stop ruling every room he enters.
